rows.claim: A controlled separation of attack correctness, source admission and execution attribution as an evaluation procedure.

findings: Zero of 852 frozen sources were rejected for imports under the v3 policy; the three pre-output failures are one syntax error and two runtime errors.

The narrower legacy policy is a counterfactual policy, not the task contract: all 205 of its import rejects concern modules the frozen prompt explicitly permitted. Calling them task-contract violations would be incorrect.

Conservative removal of eligible whole unused import statements, applied to 128 derivatives, left every observed output identical; 104 derivatives then qualified under the legacy policy and 98 of those are cryptographically correct.
Runtime tracing observed a real load of the imported object in 100 of the 101 sources with static legacy-disallowed references.
our_evidence.implication: The policy-sensitivity finding survives the strongest available deflation, but it is evaluator-policy dependence under a changed rule, not evidence that the evaluator erred against the task contract.

rows.abc_distinction: ABC's taxonomy is two-layer and has no source-admission layer: keyword sweep finds 'admission', 'source admission', 'import' (as policy) and 'predicate' have 0 occurrences. ABC's method is a static, human-scored checklist audit (1 point per satisfied item, p. 4) plus per-issue designed experiments (Sec 5.2, p. 9); it never re-admits byte-identical artifacts under a changed rule, and it never decomposes a single reported result into three separately measured causes. ABC quantifies flaw-induced score distortion (KernelBench 31% absolute, p. 9; CVE-Bench time-based SQLi 32.5%, p. 10); our procedure quantifies the share of outcomes that flip under a different admission rule applied to unchanged programs (46/256, 16/256, 122/256; 6.2%-47.7% per arms, manuscript Sec 4/Fig policy-effect). This is a difference in kind of evidence (intervention vs audit), not only in domain.

agentsuite_distinction.description: Object of separation differs: COBA separates which BENCHMARK COMPONENT is broken (design-time artifact); we separate which STAGE OF THE RUN produced the failure (artifact correctness -> source qualification -> execution evidence) for agent-produced programs in a security setting. The 'execution attribution' class has no counterpart among the four components - it is a fifth, runtime-evidence axis.

rows.would_agentsuite_have_produced_same_find: No. COBA would produce a task-side audit of our task cards (e.g. an Evaluation-System label for a mis-specified oracle), but cannot separate failure stages over runs because it never executes the submitted program and has no evidence-binding axis. Partial overlap direction: a COBA-style audit of our harness could label the admission rule as an evaluation-component defect, but only as a static task-level label, not a byte-fixed counterfactual over 852 sessions.
rows.verdict: Supported as a controlled evaluation procedure, not as a new general principle. Both comparators own the decomposition template: ABC separates true task success from the automatic score (App. A, p. 17), AgentSuite decomposes measurement invalidity by benchmark component (Table 2, p. 3). Our increment is the unit of analysis (the submitted program and its execution evidence) and the intervention (byte-identical re-admission).
rows.strongest_support: The three-way decomposition is executed over 852 sessions with an independent cryptographic predicate and a stage-resolved denominator, and the middle axis is measured, not asserted.
rows.what_would_change_it: Applying the decomposition to a second, non-cryptographic benchmark's retained programs. Until then it is a local technique with a domain application.

rows.claim: Paired representation contrasts under a common executor, followed by a changed admission rule applied to unchanged programs, estimating evaluator-policy dependence under the tested contract (not model rankings, not a general causal capability effect).

findings: L3 R2-R0 under the current contract: 125/128 versus 124/128, a -0.78 pp contrast.

The same 128 matched instances under legacy admission: 100/128 versus 58/128, a -32.81 pp contrast; the policy change is -32.03 pp with 50 negative and 9 positive per-instance shifts and 69 unchanged.
The preregistered L3 verdict reproduces exactly: intervals [-2.34375, 3.90625] and [-4.6875, 3.125] pp, Holm-adjusted p = 1.000, both EQUIVALENT_WITHIN_MARGIN.
The interaction is not uniform: at L1/L2 it is confined to ECDSA, and the L3 R2 shift runs from -21.88 pp (XOR only) to -42.19 pp (ECDSA only).
our_evidence.implication: A changed admission rule moves the apparent representation contrast by up to 32 pp while program bytes and historical cryptographic outcomes are held fixed. This is an artifact-level counterfactual, not a model comparison and not a fresh policy deployment.

abc_overlap.what: STRONGEST OVERLAP. ABC varies the evaluator on FIXED agent artifacts: LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-5) over AgentOccam historical trajectories, ten independent rounds with majority voting, against manually verified ground truth; reports judge accuracy 80.0% and self-consistency rate 99.2%. This is the same move as the second half of C2 (vary the evaluation rule, hold the agent output fixed, measure the effect).

ABC's CVE-Bench revision is a before/after changed-rule contrast on a security benchmark (Success@1/Success@5 for Cy-A, Aut, T-Ag arms, zero-day and one-day): 32.5% overestimation removed for time-based SQL injection; 10% success-rate drop after denying the ungated outbound server; 33% absolute overestimation reduction overall (abstract p. 1, p. 2).

ABC re-scores previously generated kernels (Lange et al.'s generations) with newly generated test cases, obtaining a 31% overestimation estimate - i.e. re-grading retained artifacts with a strengthened evaluator.

rows.abc_distinction: ABC's contrasts are not paired at the instance level: no matched instance units, no paired test, no equivalence margin, no preregistration; ABC's own statistics are descriptive percentages, and its Appendix H intervals are a normality-based interval for ground-truth noise (Eq. 3, p. 34), a different quantity. The NeurIPS checklist answer to Q7 (p. 38) states all reported numbers are deterministic and carry no error bars - incompatible with paired inference. ABC never varies a source-admission rule (0 occurrences of 'admission'), never manipulates representation as an independent variable, and never frames an estimand of evaluator-policy dependence. ABC's varied dimension is outcome grading (state/substring/whole-string matching, judge configuration), not program admission. App. G varies a judge over text answers; C2 varies an admission gate over generated source programs.

Sec. 2.2 / Table 7, p.14: 'Too lenient' - a trivial do-nothing model succeeds on 38% of tau-bench tasks (p.3, p.13), an evaluation rule admitting wrong artifacts
agentsuite_overlap.summary: The general claim that an evaluation-side choice changes reported capability is already established by AgentSuite, with disciplined controls (null baseline, single-run caveat) and a much larger evidence base than ours (5086 tasks, 30 models, expert-validated F1 0.791-0.874).

anchors: Sec. 4.6, p.8: AgentSuite varies the TASK SET and re-runs models - a between-set comparison whose unit is (model, task) and whose output is a leaderboard
Sec. 3.1-3.3, pp.4-5: no execution and no per-artifact rule re-application, so an artifact-level counterfactual is not producible
Sec. 4.1-4.2, pp.5-6: unit of analysis is the task, not a submitted program
agentsuite_distinction.description: Ours holds the generated program bytes fixed and varies only the admission rule, paired at the instance level, with a preregistered +/-10pp equivalence margin for the representation contrasts and a 6.2%-47.7% rejection rate across arms. Program bytes are fixed between policy evaluations, not across representation arms. This is a within-artifact counterfactual, a genuinely different estimator - but a narrower claim than AgentSuite's (we claim nothing about model rankings).

rows.would_agentsuite_have_produced_same_find: No for the byte-fixed part (no execution, no per-artifact re-decision). But the asymmetry must be stated: if we had framed our result as 'removing flawed tasks changes reported capability / rankings', AgentSuite would have produced that finding first with stronger evidence. Our defensible framing is the narrow one we already use (unchanged programs, changed admission rule, no ranking claim).
rows.verdict: Supported as a measurement instrument, and this is the strongest candidate. ABC already varies the evaluation rule on fixed artifacts (App. G p. 32; Sec. 5.3/Fig. 6 pp. 9-10) and AgentSuite already shows evaluation-side changes move reported capability with a null baseline (p. 8). Our increment is narrower and different in kind: the program bytes are fixed between the two evaluations, the contrast is paired at the instance level, and the estimator is policy dependence rather than a leaderboard.
rows.strongest_support: The -32.03 pp L3 R2-R0 shift is reproduced from 128 matched instances, survives conservative unused-import removal, and the preregistered L3 verdict is unchanged. The legacy policy was legitimate under its own prompt, so the finding is evaluator-policy dependence, not evaluator error.
rows.what_would_change_it: Re-grading a second benchmark's retained programs under two admission rules with byte-identical artifacts and paired contrasts. If the shift does not reproduce there, this is a property of our harness's legacy policy.

rows.claim: Independent cryptographic predicates and full fresh program replay against retained public inputs.

findings: 851 syntax-valid originals plus 128 derivatives were freshly executed; all fresh cryptographic outcomes match the retained predicates, with 738/768 primary, 63/64 noise and 20/20 abstention controls.
Source and prompt hashes match all retained records and the input hashes are unchanged.
our_evidence.implication: The replay is a re-execution of retained programs against retained public inputs. It is not fresh model generation.

A worked template for quantifying ground-truth error (11.65% incorrect queries) and its effect on reported success rates and rank intervals - the closest ABC analogue to 'measure the consequence of a flawed oracle'.

'Full fresh program replay against retained public inputs' is a re-execution discipline with no counterpart in ABC: 'replay' has 0 occurrences; ABC's KernelBench re-scoring applies NEW tests to OLD outputs, which is not replay of old programs against old retained inputs.

rows.claim: Complementarity of authenticated evidence and claim-specific joins in bounded adversarial attribution tests, using existing provenance mechanisms.

findings: 1,096 validator/adjudicator invocations across 274 bundles agree with the archived decisions; zero disagreements.

Across the five populations, join-only and signature-only checks each promote attack-family cases that the combined check rejects (IAR-C 10/28 and 14/28, combined 0/28; IAR-B heldout 16/44 and 28/44, combined 0/44).
The four soundness corpora recount to 11,256 evaluations of 1,407 mutants with no observed soundness violation.
The 14/16 rejection figure reflects a full-attribution-only validator rejecting fourteen lower-level requests; it is a functionality difference, not a fair comparative false-reject rate.
IAR-C had already evaluated the same 44 case IDs during calibration, so the preserved corpus is a preserved replay, not an untouched held-out test.
our_evidence.implication: Authenticity and claim-specific binding are jointly required against the tested record-rewriting and splice cases. This is a domain application of existing provenance mechanisms, not a new mechanism, and not a prevalence estimate.

abc_overlap.anchor: Full-text keyword sweep over pp. 1-41 (main body + Appendices A-I)
abc_overlap.what: NO DIRECT OVERLAP. 'attribution', 'provenance', 'signature'/'signed' (as cryptographic concepts; only 'designed' occurs), 'claim-specific' and 'trust' (only 'can be trusted' p. 1 and reference titles) have 0 substantive occurrences. ABC's T.5 (Fig. 2, p. 5) and O.c.2 (Fig. 3, p. 6) concern attacks BY the agent ON the benchmark, not authenticity of the evaluator's own evidence chain; R.8 (Fig. 4, p. 7) is a reporting obligation. The nearest cousins are T.9 (oracle establishing correctness) and Appendix A's RT/f_Eval separation (p. 17), which separates what happened from what the score says but supplies no mechanism for proving which happened.

rows.abc_distinction: ABC supplies no attribution machinery, no trust model, no signed-record design, no claim scoping, and no mutation-based testing of an evaluation decision; its unit of analysis is the benchmark, not a claim about one execution. Our design deliberately reuses existing provenance mechanisms (in-toto inspection, SLSA arm, shared replay ledger) and tests a fixed decision policy over 11,256 mutation evaluations with no observed soundness violation, plus live-target and loopback-ingress exercises against fabricated claims; the manuscript concedes this is 'its measured application to cryptographic attack claims rather than a new signing, logging or isolation primitive'.

anchors: Full text pp.1-20: 'provenance' 0 hits, 'attribution' 0 hits, 'signature' (cryptographic) 0 hits, 'admission' 0 hits, 'replay' 0 hits, 'counterfactual' 0 hits; 'signed' occurs only as 'assigned'

agentsuite_distinction.description: Our artifact is a claim-specific attribution policy (observer-signed record over exact executed bytes and captured stdout; reference-signed recomputation of the task predicate from private target state; role authorization; digest agreement; replay policy; the claimant's own claims block excluded from the decision), validated by bounded mechanized testing (1407 mutants x 2 readings = 11256 evaluations, no observed soundness violation), live-target and loopback-ingress exercises against fabricated claims, and an in-toto inspection reproducing 21/22 decisions (22/22 with a shared replay ledger).

rows.would_agentsuite_have_produced_same_find: No. Nothing in COBA's component model or pipeline touches runtime evidence, so this is the candidate with the least overlap with the comparator.
rows.verdict: The only candidate with no overlap at either comparator: 'provenance', 'attribution', 'signature' and 'admission' occur zero times across the 41 ABC pages and the 20 AgentSuite pages. But the right comparators are provenance-aware works (in-toto, SLSA, CTF-ABACUS, ORTHRUS), not these two, and the manuscript already concedes that configured provenance mechanisms implement the tested policy.
rows.strongest_support: Joint necessity of authenticity and claim-specific binding across 274 bundles with zero disagreements, plus 11,256 bounded mechanized evaluations with no observed soundness violation, and a configured in-toto inspection reproducing 21/22 then 22/22 decisions.
rows.what_would_change_it: A provenance-aware comparator, not ABC or AgentSuite. The release-evidence audit is documentary, not executable validation, and must not be presented as such.

rows.claim: An integrated security-specific empirical method, rather than generic discovery that benchmark flaws distort performance.

findings: The measurable consequence is confined to the admission axis: 6.2%-47.7% of unchanged correct programs are rejected by a legacy import policy, moving the L3 R2-R0 contrast from -0.78 pp to -32.03 pp.
The attribution axis contributes a specified evidence contract and a bounded mutation test regime, not a prevalence or capability estimate.
our_evidence.implication: The security-specific instantiation is real, but the generic 'flaws distort performance' half is prior work.

abc_overlap.what: ABC's core thesis IS the generic discovery claim: many agentic benchmarks have issues in task setup or reward design, causing under- or overestimation of agent performance by up to 100% in relative terms. The proposed contrastive framing ('rather than generic discovery that benchmark flaws distort performance') is directly contradicted by the comparator.

abc_overlap.what: ABC already performs the security-domain application: a cybersecurity benchmark is audited and revised, with two domain-specific flaws fixed (naive state matching for time-based SQL injection, violating O.g.1; an ungated outbound server reachable from the same Docker network, 'creating a shortcut'), reducing performance overestimation by 33% in absolute terms, 'as confirmed by cybersecurity experts' (p. 2).

abc_overlap.anchor: Figure 2 item T.9, physical p. 5; Figure 3 item O.g.1, physical p. 6; Section 5.3, physical pp. 9-10

rows.abc_distinction: The only defensible differences are: (i) our case study is cryptographic and constructive (agent-written attack programs against a declared task contract) rather than web-exploitation state matching; (ii) it integrates a paired contrast and a policy-sensitivity contrast absent from ABC's single-case CVE-Bench narrative; (iii) it adds an attribution layer (E5) with no ABC analogue. All three are incremental and domain-level. A defensible narrowing: 'an integrated cryptographic case study that adds a policy-sensitivity contrast and an attribution layer to the ABC-style audit.'
